subject: Banking
title: Why Banking Regulation Exists
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Why Banking Regulation Exists.

hook.text: Before deposit insurance, bank runs were common. A rumor could destroy a healthy bank overnight as depositors fled.

buildup.text: The 1930s saw 9,000 US banks fail. Savings vanished. The government created the FDIC to guarantee deposits.

discovery.text: Regulation ensures banks hold enough capital, manage risk, and treat customers fairly.

twist.text: Silicon Valley Bank collapsed in 2023 despite regulations. Supervisors saw the risks but acted too slowly.

climax.text: Regulation cannot prevent every crisis. But without it, crises would be constant.

punchline.text: 9,000 banks failed in the 1930s. Regulation prevents most, not all, failures.

quiz.question: Why was the FDIC created?
options: To guarantee bank deposits after 9,000 banks failed in the 1930s

details.summary: Banking regulation exists because banks hold public deposits, create money through lending, and are interconnected in ways that mean one bank's failure can cascade through the entire economy. Without regulation, bank runs and crises would be routine.
details.whyItMatters: Every banking crisis in history has been followed by new regulation, and every period of deregulation has eventually led to a new crisis. Understanding this cycle is essential for evaluating current debates about fintech regulation.
takeaways: Deposit insurance prevents bank runs by guaranteeing customer deposits
Capital requirements ensure banks can absorb losses without collapsing
The regulation-deregulation cycle has repeated for over two centuries

faq.question: What is the most important banking regulation?
faq.answer: Deposit insurance, created in the US in 1933 through the FDIC. By guaranteeing deposits up to a limit, it eliminated the incentive for depositors to panic and withdraw money during uncertainty, ending the cycle of devastating bank runs.

faq.question: Do fintech companies need the same regulation as banks?
faq.answer: This is the central debate. Fintechs argue regulation stifles innovation. Regulators argue that any company performing bank-like functions should meet bank-like safety standards. The answer likely lies in proportional, activity-based regulation.
